opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think my view has evolved over time. For a long stretch the dominant recipe was basically "more data, more compute, bigger models," and that worked remarkably well. But at some point you have to ask what happens when the easy, high-quality data starts running out. Then data efficiency stops being a nice-to-have and becomes one of the central problems.

The way I think about it, humans are incredibly data efficient. A kid doesn't need to read trillions of tokens to reason about the world. That gap tells you something: either our models are missing some inductive bias, or the learning objective or the way we present data is suboptimal. Probably both.

In practice I see a few levers. One is just better data: curation, filtering, mixture design. People underestimate how much of the gains come from simply getting the data mix right. Another is the objective itself. I've always been interested in whether plain next-token prediction is the most efficient way to extract signal, or whether mixing in denoising-style objectives, or other ways of corrupting and reconstructing, gets you more out of every token. The third, which is getting a lot of attention now, is using compute at training and inference time to generate signal: synthetic data, self-play, RL on verifiable tasks. In a sense you're trading compute for data.

So I don't think data efficiency alone gets you to AGI, but I think it's increasingly going to be the bottleneck that separates teams. Everyone has access to roughly the same internet. The question is who can squeeze the most intelligence out of it, and that's partly a research question and partly just really careful engineering and taste.

r001.rationale: The response frames data efficiency as a central challenge and points to alternative objectives, inductive biases, and data-use methods as ways to extract more learning signal toward AGI.

r002.rationale: It says children can reason about the world with far less data than models, but does not state that young children exceed LLMs on any tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, actually. The honest answer is that data efficiency is probably one of the most underrated axes right now, because everyone's been so fixated on scale. And scale works — I'm not going to pretend otherwise, I spent years at Google watching it work. But if you look at the trajectory, we're kind of running into the wall where the easy data is gone. The high-quality tokens on the internet are finite, and we've basically eaten most of them.

So the question becomes: what do you do when you can't just throw more tokens at the problem? And I think there are a few things. One is that the architecture and the training recipe actually matter more than people give them credit for. There was this period where everyone said "architecture doesn't matter, just scale the transformer," and I think that's been somewhat true at the margin, but it's also a bit of a cop-out. When you're data-constrained, the inductive biases you bake in — how you handle long context, how you do mixture-of-experts, how you structure the objective — those things start to show up again.

The second thing is that I think the field conflates data efficiency with sample efficiency in the narrow sense, like fewer examples to learn a task. But the more interesting version is: how much can you get out of a token? Humans don't see a trillion tokens before they're useful. They see way less, but they get a lot more signal per token because there's grounding, there's interaction, there's feedback. So things like RL, synthetic data, self-play — those aren't just tricks to generate more data, they're ways to extract more learning per unit of experience. And I think that's actually closer to what a path to AGI looks like than just pretraining on everything ever written.

The third thing, and this is maybe a bit contrarian, is that I don't think data efficiency alone gets you there. It's necessary but not sufficient. If you had a perfectly data-efficient learner, you'd still need the right curriculum, the right environments, the right objectives. So I see it as one leg of the stool. You need compute, you need good data, and you need a learner that doesn't waste what you give it. Right now most of the progress has come from the first two, and I think the next few years are going to be about the third one catching up.

r001.rationale: The response treats data efficiency as a route toward AGI and discusses alternative learning approaches—such as grounding, interaction, feedback, RL, synthetic data, and self-play—as ways to learn more from each token.

r002.rationale: It compares human learning with large language model training in general, but does not mention young children or say they exceed LLMs at any tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think data efficiency is a really important lens, because getting better by consuming more data is different from getting better at learning. If a system needs enormous numbers of examples to pick up something that a person can learn from a few interactions, there’s still a gap worth understanding.

But I wouldn’t make data efficiency the sole criterion for AGI. You also want to know whether the model can transfer what it learns, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and make use of feedback. Learning something from a few examples is much more compelling if you can then apply it outside the setting where you learned it.

So the question for me is: how much new capability can you extract from a given amount of experience? Scaling can still help, but I’d want to see progress in that learning process itself.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes improving learning efficiency toward AGI, but does not frame that pursuit as a search for new learning paradigms.

r002.rationale: It does not mention young children or compare their learning ability and data use with LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data efficiency is a really important lens, because it asks whether we’re actually getting better at learning, rather than just giving models more information. Scaling data has been very effective, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us how much experience a system needs to acquire a new capability.

Humans can often learn something from a few examples by connecting it to things they already know. Of course, that comparison is tricky, because humans come with a lot of prior experience. For models, the interesting question is similar: once you’ve built a strong foundation, how efficiently can you learn something new and generalize beyond the examples you’ve seen?

I wouldn’t say data efficiency alone gets us to AGI. But if we can get more capability out of the same data through better objectives, architectures, or ways of learning, that feels like meaningful progress. It also gives us another direction beyond simply making the training run bigger.

r001.rationale: It frames data efficiency as improving how models learn and generalize, including through better objectives, architectures, or learning methods, as progress toward AGI.

r002.rationale: It compares models with humans generally, but does not mention young children, LLMs being outperformed on specific tasks, or the smaller amount of data children use.
